data.title: Jennings: Ramaswamy's campaign tactics 'worst politics you could imagine'
data.description:
Republican commentator Scott Jennings took a swipe at Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) for using a controversial campaign ad featuring his opponent’s estranged mother.

The ad, which Ramaswamy’s campaign is now spending $4 million to broadcast statewide, features Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, accusing Acton of being a “liar” her whole life.

Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12 after her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her. Arthur remained with Acton’s stepfather until his death.

According to legal filings Acton’s campaign shared with The Hill, Arthur was previously convicted with theft and animal cruelty, though one of her sentences was vacated.

Jennings, a Trump ally who frequently defends the president and the GOP on CNN, joins a growing list of Republicans pushing back against the ad.

The conservative political commentator told CNN’s Anderson Cooper Friday that the ad is “not good” morally and is a political misstep.

“What you’re talking about here is Amy Acton’s mother is basically saying, ‘I don’t trust 12-year-old Amy Acton, who was quite possibly raped in my own home, to be governor,’” Jennings said. “It’s a ludicrous sort of argument that they’re making.”

“This is probably the worst politics you could imagine, and it’s bringing a lot of attention to Amy Acton’s story, her narrative,” he added.

Ramaswamy has doubled down on the ad, accusing Acton of “lying about an ad that is about lying.” President Trump and Vice President Vance have repeatedly defended the Ohio Republican, with Vance saying he was “disgusted” by those in his party who criticized use of the ad.

Trump continues to say that he trusts Acton’s mother, and told reporters at the White House Friday that he did not “know anything about a stepfather,” telling the reporter who asked the question to be “quiet.”

“Vivek should keep it up,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday.

Jennings said the White House “absolutely” could brief the president on Acton’s side of the story.

”I don’t know what he knows or what he doesn’t know,” Jennings said. “They absolutely could [brief him], and if they did, he would learn the terrible details of this.”

Polling suggests Acton’s lead in the gubernatorial race was already growing ahead of the scandal, and nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Acton a 62 percent chance of beating Ramaswamy.

Jennings said the ad could have backfired because it does not help the former presidential candidate’s likability, which the CNN commentator said is one of his biggest challenges in this election.

“One of Ramaswamy’s key candidate deficiencies is likability. Not certain this is doing anything to help that,” Jennings said. “It was a problem for him in the ‘24 presidential primary, and it’s a problem for him in this governor’s race.”

data.title: Ukraine reports Starlink operating again after slowdown
data.description:
Ukraine’s Starlink satellite links have been restored after the country experienced limitations with accessing this critical technology, the Ukrainian defense minister said Saturday. 

SpaceX’s military-grade version of Starlink, called Starshield, supports Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. 

Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters on a call that the ministry’s monitoring systems now reported stable connections for objects traveling faster than around 250 miles per hour. 

“The Ministry of Defence’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield,” Khmara told reporters, according to Reuters. “We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable.”

Khmara attributed the change to “direct dialogue” between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Trump administration. He added that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.” 

This announcement follows tensions between Kyiv and the U.S. over President Trump’s Russian diesel deal and decision to postpone sanctions on Moscow — two decisions Zelensky warned endangered Ukrainians in their ongoing war against Russia. 

Zelensky said in Friday remarks that Ukraine’s military was still struggling with Starlink satellite speeds limited at around 100 mph. 

“The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there, and the speed has not been restored,” the Ukrainian president said. 

Earlier that day, Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn that he had not spoken with SpaceX leader Elon Musk about the restricted Starlink speeds in Ukraine but said he “might have to” if the issue was not fixed. 

This week, Russia accepted an invitation to resume three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the U.S.

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” to restart talks after Nov. 10, according to his foreign affairs adviser. 

Additionally, the White House said Friday that first lady Melania Trump helped secure a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that will begin Thursday in the front-line city of Oleshky. 

This action will “allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway,” according to the White House.

data.title: Critics should do their homework before attacking Arabic language programs
data.description:
I expected criticism when I agreed to consult with the Embassy of Qatar on its education initiatives. But I did not foresee the torrent of falsehoods that would come.

Qatar plays an important and sometimes complicated role in the Middle East. I thought my experience as a former secretary of Education could help clarify at least that part of its activities. I did not expect a Qatari program that helps American students learn Arabic to be portrayed as an effort to “infiltrate” our public schools.

That is the argument being advanced by organizations that have raised concerns about Qatar Foundation International, which provided grants to support Arabic language programs in American schools. The fact is, America needs more language education, not less. And scrutiny needs to yield to the facts.

Under the Qatar Foundation International program, American schools retained control of what was taught. The funding was transparent. Students got a legitimate educational opportunity to learn a new language. They got only that and nothing more. 

Critics cite an instance from P.S. 261 in Brooklyn where a classroom map labeled the area of Israel as Palestine. Qatar Foundation International had supported an Arab language program at the school, and the map quickly became part of a larger narrative about Qatari influence.

But there is an important difference between funding a program and supplying a particular classroom item. New York City Schools Chancellor David Banks testified before Congress that the teacher, a New York City employee, had obtained the map with her own funds while visiting Jerusalem. The map had nothing to do with Qatar Foundation International.

The same is true in New Haven, Connecticut, where Qatar Foundation International has supported Arabic instruction since 2018. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies includes New Haven in its exposé-style presentation that frames foreign-language education grants as a national security and foreign influence threat.

But Mayor Justin Elicker and Superintendent Madeline Negrón looked into the claims. Elicker said publicly that he had examined the program extensively and found that it was “purely teaching students Arabic.”

In June, Qatar Foundation International announced that it was ending operations in the U.S. after 17 years of supporting Arabic language education. Schools and teachers that relied on its grants will have to look elsewhere to sustain those programs. Some critics, including an official from the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy, celebrated the news.

That reaction is deeply misguided. American students need more opportunities to study strategically important languages. The disappearance of funding for Arabic instruction is nothing to celebrate.

The bipartisan Commission on Language Learning of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences concluded that language skills matter to America’s economic competitiveness, national security and ability to engage with the world. It recommended that every child should have the opportunity to learn a language other than English. It also suggested that partnerships involving schools, governments, philanthropies, businesses and communities make that possible.

Arabic is one of the world’s most widely spoken languages and is important to U.S. diplomacy, national security and business.

Germany’s government supports German language programs in hundreds of American schools. Spain’s Ministry of Education places Spanish language assistants in schools across the U.S. Italy offers grants that help cover the salaries of Italian language teachers. Japan supports Japanese language instruction and sends teaching assistants to American schools.

We do not describe these programs as attempts to infiltrate American classrooms. We recognize them for what they are: countries promoting their languages and schools taking advantage of resources that expand opportunities for students.

Arabic should be treated no differently. In fact, Qatar Foundation International’s grants were indeed no different. They provided resources to teach an important language to American students. And that’s all.

Outside funding of Arabic language studies should be transparent, of course. School districts should control the curriculum. Parents should know what is being taught. Political or religious indoctrination has no place in a public-school language class.

I come to this debate with some personal experience.

I recently resigned from the Middle East Media Research Institute. I once strongly supported its mission of bringing greater transparency to Middle Eastern discourse by translating and publishing primary-source material. But in my view, the organization has moved too far from that mission and toward ideological advocacy, including in its treatment of Qatar and the promotion of conspiratorial reports about the nation.

Arabic should not be treated differently from German, Spanish, Italian or Japanese because of contemporary politics. America will not become stronger by giving its children fewer opportunities to understand the world. We need transparency and, of course, we need local control.

But most importantly, we need more language education, not less.

William J. Bennett is a former secretary of Education.

data.title: Early voting surges in battleground states as Democrats outpace GOP gains
data.description:
Early voting is surging in several key battleground states, giving Democrats hope that their strength in midterm polling could translate into a turnout advantage in November.

In North Carolina, more than 1.2 million early ballots have been accepted, a 37 percent increase from the same point leading up to the 2022 midterms, according to an analysis released Friday by Catawba College political scientist Michael Bitzer. 

That growth — which includes both in-person and mail-in ballots — has been driven by a 47 percent increase among registered Democrats and a 60 percent increase in participation among unaffiliated voters. Early voting among Republicans is up 2.6 percent.

Similar patterns are emerging elsewhere, with high turnout especially pronounced in historically Republican-leaning states with competitive Senate races this cycle.

More than 23 million ballots have been accepted nationwide, compared with more than 15 million reported at a similar point ahead of the 2022 midterms. In Kansas, early voting is up roughly 69 percent, while it’s up 41 percent in Maine and 24 percent in Iowa, according to a New York Times analysis of state election records and voter data through Thursday.

Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political science professor who tracks early voting, said Democrats and unaffiliated voters are similarly outpacing Republicans in turnout gains compared to 2022 across states where he has comparable party registration data — including Kansas, Maine, Iowa and Nebraska.

“It’s the same pattern. Democrats and unaffiliateds are engaged. Republicans are not as engaged,” McDonald told The Hill, adding, “And it explains why you might be seeing this shift of the battleground into these red states. Overall, there’s just more engagement among Democrats.”

McDonald cautioned that there is a range of factors that can affect states’ early voting numbers, including changing timelines for when mail-in ballots are sent out. 

There are also limits to what early voting data can reveal. Not all states record party registration, and there’s no guarantee that a voter’s party affiliation will match that of the candidate they choose to support.

But McDonald said the early voting patterns give credence to polls showing Democrats in a strong position heading into Election Day.

“The early voting data is just telling me that what we know from the polling data is correct. That yes, the polling is not telling us something wrong. There’s not some big polling miss on the horizon,” McDonald said.

In Texas, Democrats are hoping Senate nominee James Talarico can end the party’s more than three-decade drought in statewide elections. But Texas does not register voters by party, making it harder to determine whether Democrats’ strength in polling is translating into an early turnout advantage. 

Decision Desk HQ’s modeling suggests a narrower partisan gap than in some other states. Of the 2.06 million ballots cast in person or returned by mail as of Thursday, an estimated 44.3 percent came from Democratic voters and 43.7 percent came from Republicans. Among Hispanic early voters, the model estimates Democrats outnumber Republicans by roughly 2.5 to 1. 

Democrats are also pointing to strong participation in Travis County, a Democratic stronghold that includes Austin. 

More than 158,000 in-person ballots were cast during the first four days of early voting, up roughly 61 percent from the same point in 2022 and 19 percent from 2018, according to a compilation of state election data provided by the county Democratic Party. The county’s registered electorate has also grown since 2018, so the increase in ballots does not necessarily represent a higher participation rate. 

“In Travis County, where Democrats really need to run up the score, we’re beating 2022 and 2018 turnout levels—elections when Beto [O’Rourke] was on the ballot—and pacing towards 2024 turnout,” Luke Warford, chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said in a statement to The Hill.

But higher turnout in Democratic strongholds alone will not be enough for Talarico to win in November, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston. 

“Democrats don’t just need high turnout to win statewide. They need urban margins large enough to overcome rural margins, and Republicans’ rural floor has risen since 2018,” Rottinghaus said. “High turnout is necessary for Democrats, but not sufficient.”

He also noted that high turnout this cycle is “not only a Democratic story,” saying there’s a “slight purple tinge to the turnout so far,” and redder, rural areas are “slow out of the gate but catching up.”

In Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is favored to fend off his Republican challenger, voters also do not register by party, “so we can only make guesses about who is turning out to vote based on geography and demographic factors,” said Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at Emory University.

Early voting is slightly higher this year, with approximately 1.5 million ballots cast through Thursday, up from roughly 1.4 million at the same point in 2022, according to the Times analysis. 

Gillespie said Democrats likely benefit from elevated turnout among Black voters and among voters living in the metropolitan areas of Atlanta, Athens, Savannah, Macon and Augusta. But she said participation is also strong in traditionally Republican areas, like Cherokee and Forsyth counties.

“Democrats have been trying to make inroads there, so it is not clear whether the people turning out are Democrats or Republicans yet,” she said. 

In Virginia, where Democrats are targeting several GOP-held House seats, nearly 930,000 early ballots had been cast through Thursday, roughly 80 percent more than at the same point in 2022, according to the Virginia Public Access Project.

“Early voting in Virginia has been concentrated in congressional districts where Republicans are playing defense, not offense,” University of Mary Washington political scientist Stephen Farnsworth said. 

He noted that, although Virginians do not register by party, “polling shows far more interest in voting among Democrats than Republicans.”

Several factors could still influence turnout in the next week. Republicans have time to narrow the participation gap, and GOP voters have historically turned out more heavily on Election Day. 

President Trump’s shifting message on mail-in ballots could also affect voter behavior. He has repeatedly attacked and tried to restrict mail voting but has more recently encouraged Republicans to vote early or by mail.

“The big question this year is whether Republicans are more likely to take advantage of early voting now that President Trump has relaxed his rhetoric about why one should only vote on Election Day,” Gillespie said. “If Republicans vote alongside Democrats in early voting, then we may not see Election Day surges in voting in Republican areas that we have seen in the past.”

McDonald, meanwhile, said concerns about mail voting could push some Democrats to vote in person, reducing the likelihood of their ballots being rejected. More than half a million mail ballots were rejected for various reasons in 2024, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. 

“If there are fewer people who are voting by mail, and it’s particularly Democrats, that means that there are going to be fewer Democratic rejected mail ballots,” McDonald said.

“Trump may have inadvertently done a favor to the Democrats by encouraging their voters to vote in person, and we’re seeing that in the in-person early voting.”

data.title: Why a blue wave might miss Minnesota's Senate race
data.description:
Political headwinds are blowing in Democrats’ favor nationally, with high gas prices and President Trump’s record-low approval rating creating a difficult midterm environment for Republicans. 

But in Minnesota’s open Senate race to replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D), Democrats are facing an unexpectedly competitive race. 

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) holds a slim lead over former sports reporter Michele Tafoya (R) that’s only narrowed, according to limited public polls ahead of Election Day. 

Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report recently shifted the race in the GOP’s favor — from “likely” to “lean” Democrat, citing Flanagan’s underperformance in polling compared to Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D), who is running for governor, a statewide fraud scandal and Republicans notching a strong recruit in Tafoya.

And while Tafoya has an uphill battle in a state that has not elected a Republican to the Senate in nearly 25 years, Flanagan’s biggest political vulnerability stems from her nearly eight years serving under Gov. Tim Walz (D). 

“This is one of the races that could be so close we might have a recount,” said longtime Minnesota political analyst Blois Olson, who called Flanagan’s proximity to the fraud scandal “a little bit like ankle weights around her campaign.” 

The sprawling welfare fraud scandal that has engulfed the Walz administration has become a major pain point for the progressive candidate. 

Walz abandoned his reelection bid for a third term in January as the allegations of up to billions of dollars in fraud within Minnesota social service programs attracted criticism both in Minnesota and nationally. Flanagan, Walz’s running mate in 2018 and 2022, is one of few in the Walz administration facing voters this November.

Republicans are hoping voters’ frustrations over the administration’s handling of fraud and the anti-incumbency wave will extend to the lieutenant governor, with no incumbent running for governor or the Senate. 

“Peggy Flanagan allowed fraudsters to plunder billions in taxpayer dollars on her watch, and now she’s facing questions about her own inflated academic record,” Bernadette Breslin, a spokeswoman for the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, said in a statement to The Hill. “Minnesotans aren’t buying the excuses Flanagan is selling, and they’re counting on Michele Tafoya to protect their hard-earned tax dollars.”  

Tafoya has made the fraud scandal a central part of her campaign, arguing that Flanagan and the rest of the Walz administration should be held accountable for failures that occurred during her tenure. 

“Why has no one been fired?” Tafoya said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal. “The only real consequence we’ve seen is that Tim Walz was convinced to step out of his third term gubernatorial race because there was no way he was going to survive this. But Peggy Flanagan’s asking for a promotion.” 

Even aspects of Flanagan’s personal background have been more heavily scrutinized in recent weeks. The Wall Street Journal initially reported earlier this week that the Minnesota progressive had not been a member of the Phi Beta Kappa honors society, with the campaign saying that while Flanagan was nominated, she couldn’t afford the membership fee. 

However, the honor society later provided The Hill and other news outlets a statement, which confirmed she had been a member. The campaign told The Hill that the newspaper’s questions over her status with the honor society prompted internal confusion, and they weren’t able to offer confirmation of her membership to the Journal in time for publication. 

Flanagan’s campaign pushed back on Tafoya over her handling of the statewide fraud scandal, pointing to the distinction between the governor’s and the lieutenant governor’s responsibilities. 

A campaign official said Walz oversees state agencies and programs, while Flanagan’s statutory duties are more limited. 

The official acknowledged that more should have been done sooner to address the fraud and that the issue was personal for Flanagan, who relied on Medicaid and Section 8 housing at one point in her life. 

The Tafoya campaign did not respond to a request for comment from The Hill. 

While the widespread fraud scandal has put Flanagan on the defensive, Tafoya also faces a political liability of her own with Trump’s souring popularity in the state and as the price of items like gas and fertilizer have shot up amid an ongoing war with Iran and a tariff war with Canada. 

Uproar over Trump’s federal immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, which led to two U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)-involved shootings, has also complicated Tafoya’s efforts to balance her appeal to both Trump’s steady voter base and independent voters who may be more reluctant to support Republicans in statewide elections. 

“The fraud thing — that it hangs over the state of Minnesota — certainly is a bit of a drag for Democrats, but at the same time, the Trump administration, I still think, is a bigger drag on the Republicans,” said former Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DLF) Party chair Mike Erlandson. 

Tafoya has taken steps in recent weeks to distance herself from the president. 

When asked for a reaction to the president’s endorsement at a Monday night debate, Tafoya said, “There is one endorsement that I care about and that is the one that happens on Nov. 3.” 

Tafoya criticized the president over the war in Iran during a recent interview with CBS News, saying “the war in Iran has gone on longer than I think people were ready for and we’re suffering at the gas pump.” Earlier this year, the GOP candidate caught flak for suggesting people should make “one less trip to Starbucks” to save on gas, and that the country should be supporting its military while it’s engaged in the conflict.

In a midterm environment that historically serves as a referendum on the party in power, Democrats have made no secret about tying Tafoya to Trump and the national GOP. 

A Flanagan campaign official pointed out that Tafoya “earned” her endorsement from Trump by being loyal to him and his policies, noting her support of him in the past. 

“In the last month before the election, she wants to try and walk away from all the positions that she’s been holding for years,” the spokesperson told The Hill, arguing that her recent stepping away from the president was inconsistent with her earlier positions. 

And national Democrats feel confident about their odds of keeping the state within the fold give their recent track record. They point out, too, that national Republican groups have spent little money on the contest, which they say is an acknowledgement from within the GOP that the race isn’t in play.

“Republicans haven’t won a Minnesota Senate race in more than 20 years and that losing streak will continue in 2026 when Minnesotans elect Democrat Peggy Flanagan,” Maddy McDaniel, a spokeswoman for the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm, who dubbed Tafoya as “a Trump loyalist and a wealthy Republican activist.” 

Some Republicans say the anti-incumbent energy could hit the parties either way. 

“We have also a large number of undecideds in these polls, and I think they’re truly undecided because I think that it depends on the day,” said former GOP Minnesota Senate Majority Leader Amy Frederiksen, who’s not working on the Senate race. 

“They go and fill up their tank, and they’re ticked off about Iran and tariffs,” she said, adding that “the next news story they see is … another 10 million or another 15 million stolen, and nobody did anything about it,” referring to the statewide fraud scandal.

data.title: DNI warned Rubio of 'advanced' Iranian efforts to target US personnel, memo shows
data.description:
Iranian plots to target and kill U.S. officials in the Middle East have “substantially increased,” according to a declassified intelligence memo dated Friday, with these efforts reportedly reaching “advanced stages.”

The warning, addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, came days after the State Department ordered the departure of certain nonessential U.S. personnel from Saudi Arabia as the Iran-backed Houthis ramped up attacks inside the country.

“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel,” Clayton wrote. “The lethal plotting efforts by Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”

The memo was first reported on by Axios, and a U.S. official confirmed its existence to The Hill’s broadcasting partner, NewsNation. Clayton’s message to Rubio does not mention the State Department’s evacuation of some American personnel from the Middle East.

The Houthis have attacked civilian infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, including multiple attacks on airports, which have wounded and killed civilians. Saudi officials said Wednesday its military prevented another attack on the holy city of Medina.

The strikes are part of an ongoing war between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. 

“As the Department has repeatedly emphasized, the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area,” a State Department spokesperson told The Hill Wednesday when asked about the decision to pull diplomats from the region.

U.S. military action in Islamic Republic has amplified the impact of the Yemen civil war throughout the Persian Gulf, as the Iran-backed Houthis have directly attacked countries in the region since its start. Saudi Arabia, due to its partnerships with the US, has been a target of much of the Houthi offensive.

data.title: Rubio floats CIA 'partnership' to Cubans tired of 'failed promises, corruption'
data.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered Cubans a discreet CIA partnership opportunity in a Friday social media post, saying “now is the time” for those looking to “create positive change” in the Caribbean country.

“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said in a post to the social platform X.

The U.S. government has offered CIA partnerships to residents of adversarial countries in the past, namely in Russia — where the agency launched a Telegram campaign in 2023 to encourage intelligence sharing.

Rubio’s post came after Trump again suggested the U.S. could take military action in Cuba at a rally in Fort Myers, Fla.

“We’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran,” Trump said. “Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re gonna send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

The president’s rhetoric on Cuba has escalated throughout the year. In March, Trump said “Cuba is next” after the Iran war and that he would have the “honor” of taking over the country.

The island nation has struggled with blackouts and supply shortages as the Trump administration has increased pressure on its communist regime through sanctions and an oil blockade. Rubio said last month that Cuba was a “failed state.”

“Well, the truth is Cuba has already fallen,” Rubio told Fox New commentator Sean Hannity.

Still, it is unclear whether Trump plans to follow up on his threats of military action against Cuba. Throughout the Iran war, the president has threatened to destroy the Islamic Republic’s energy infrastructure and once warned “a whole civilization” would die unless “something revolutionarily wonderful” happened before a time limit he set — only for the U.S. to back off before the deadline.

data.title: Peltola calls Alaska lawsuit a 'desperate attempt' for GOP to 'cling to power'
data.description:
Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola (D) responded to the Justice Department’s (DOJ) lawsuit seeking to block her state from certifying its election results should her Republican challenger lose, saying Friday the move was “frivolous.”

“This is clearly corruption. This is clearly a very desperate attempt to cling to power, using his allies in Washington, D.C. to rig the system even further,” Peltola, a former member of Congress, told MS NOW’s Nicolle Wallace.

The DOJ filed a lawsuit Friday seeking to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate race if anyone other than Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan wins. The department claimed that, since another candidate shares the same name as the GOP senator, the election results may be inaccurate.

The ballot includes Sen. Sullivan’s Republican affiliation and incumbent status to differentiate him from the other candidate in question, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” the filing reads.

Peltola said Friday she believes Alaska voters can tell the difference between the two candidates on the ballot and any argument otherwise is “not playing well with Alaskans.”

“It’s sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they’re voting for and what the implications of their vote is,” Peltola said.

The Center for Election Innovation and Research (CEIR), a nonprofit aiming to build confidence in U.S. elections, called the DOJ’s lawsuit “an unprecedented intervention.”

“This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election,” CEIR Executive Director David Becker said in a statement. “The DOJ attempting to intervene at this late stage is entirely against department policy.”

Democrats widely condemned the move, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who called the lawsuit an “outrage” in a post to the social platform X Friday evening.

“This is an outrage. It shows they know they’re going to lose. We will fight tooth and nail. And we will win,” Schumer wrote.

The former Alaska lawmaker said she was not sure whether Sullivan supported the DOJ’s legal strategy. In an earlier statement sent to The Hill, the incumbent senator’s campaign spokesperson Nate Adams said his team would “let the DOJ complaint run its course.”

The president has repeatedly amplified unsubstantiated mass voter fraud claims, namely toward blue states. A new poll from the New York Times/Siena University found half of Americans believe Republicans may attempt to overturn the midterm results through illegal means.

Peltola there has never been a reason to doubt the security of Alaska’s election system.

“We’ve been running great elections for decades.  There have never really been any abnormalities or irregularities to speak of,” Peltola said. “I have total confidence in Alaskans’ ability to know who they’re voting for.”

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Peltola a 61 percent chance of winning the Alaska Senate race.

data.title: Kennedy rolls out US-caught seafood labeling, Seafood.gov
data.description:
The Trump administration unveiled new initiatives for U.S. fishermen Friday, including a new government website known as Seafood.gov.

At a rally in Fort Myers, Fla., Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the creation of a voluntary label made for U.S.-caught fish, which the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began offering Friday, the White House said.

Kennedy said at the rally that fish caught in the U.S. is of higher quality than European-caught and imported seafood.

“No European country will take them, so they ship them all over here,” Kennedy said, referring to shrimp. “President Trump is rebuilding the infrastructure, he’s reopening the markets for our commercial fishermen.”

Data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows that in 2023, an estimated 80 percent of fish consumed in the U.S. was imported from other countries.

The New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association (NEFSA) reacted to Kennedy’s announcement, saying in a statement shared to the social platform X that the U.S.-made label is a “major win” for Americans.

“We believe U.S. seafood is the most sustainably harvested in the world, and this label gives consumers a simple, recognizable way to identify American-caught seafood while supporting our domestic fishing, processing, and retail industries,” NEFSA director of advocacy Jason Joyce said.

The new fishing initiative comes after the president’s trade war with Canada ruffled feathers with some in the industry.

The Maine Lobstermen’s Association said in August it feared becoming “collateral damage” in the trade war because Canada purchases large quantities of lobster from Maine fisheries.

data.title: About half concerned Republicans could try to overturn midterm results: Survey
data.description:
A new poll released Friday suggests half of Americans are concerned Republicans may try to overturn the results of November’s midterm election.

Fifty percent of respondents to the New York Times/Siena University survey said they were either “very” or “somewhat worried” the GOP may use “illegal means” to overturn the election, compared to 49 percent who are either “not too worried” or “not at all worried.”

A strong majority of Democrats — 86 percent — were among the share of likely voters who reported feeling worry about potential GOP election interference, and 52 percent independents felt the same. Even 10 percent of Republicans say they are worried their own party would overturn the results.

NYT/Siena also asked respondents if they feared Democrats may overturn the results, and 31 percent said they were — a group mainly consisting of Republicans.

Still, similar shares of Democratic, Republican and independents respondents to the NYT/Siena poll said they trusted midterm results would be accurate. And, across all parties, likely voters’ trust reached 74 percent.

President Trump has pushed claims of voter fraud for years, mainly when he or his party loses. Courts and election officials have consistently debunked or found no evidence for claims of widespread fraud in U.S. elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters Thursday the Justice Department (DOJ) has no intention “to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.” However, he did not rule out the potential for the DOJ to intervene in or block states from verifying election results.

On Friday morning, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

The DOJ argued that, because another candidate with the same name is on the ballot, the election is not fair and could confuse voters. Sen. Sullivan is identified on the ballot with his Republican and incumbent status to differentiate himself from the other Dan Sullivan.

The poll was conducted Oct. 12-19 among 3,494 likely voters nationwide. The margin of error is 1.9 percentage points
